drills.q: Name the 11 GoF behavioral patterns and classify each as 'fully absorbed by the language', 'still commonly built explicitly', or 'real but rare.'
drills.a: Absorbed: Strategy (function param), Iterator (generator), Template Method (overriding). Still built explicitly: State, Observer, Command, Chain of Responsibility. Mechanics absorbed but still earns its keep in stable-type/growing-ops domains: Visitor. Real but rare: Mediator, Memento, Interpreter.

drills.q: Distinguish Strategy from State with a concrete example of each.
drills.a: Strategy: the caller supplies the algorithm per call with no persistent identity, e.g. sorted(data, key=lambda x: -x). State: the object itself owns which behavior applies and it changes as a side effect of lifecycle events, e.g. an Order object whose valid next transitions depend on whether it's PENDING, PAID, or SHIPPED.

drills.q: An event bus subscriber throws mid-notification and every subscriber registered after it stops receiving events. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The publish loop is propagating the exception instead of isolating it per-handler, so one bad subscriber aborts the whole fan-out. Fix: wrap each handler call in its own try/except, log the failure, and continue to the next handler -- the publisher's job is fan-out, not all-or-nothing execution.

drills.q: Explain when Visitor still earns its keep over match/switch pattern matching, and when pattern matching wins instead.
drills.a: Visitor wins when the type set is fixed/stable and the set of operations grows over time (e.g. a compiler's AST with many passes) -- each new operation is a self-contained visitor class touching zero existing node classes. Pattern matching wins when operations are fixed/few but types grow, since adding a new type only needs new cases added to the (few) match sites, not a new class satisfying every existing visitor interface.

drills.q: Why doesn't Command collapse into a plain function the way Strategy does, even though both wrap behavior?
drills.a: A function call can't be queued, serialized, logged with actor/timestamp, retried, or undone without extra machinery bolted on. Making the action a first-class object with execute()/undo() gives all of that for free -- the object-ness is only worth its cost when at least one of those needs (queueing, logging, undo) is real; otherwise Command degenerates to a function call same as Strategy.

drills.q: Why were java.util.Observer/Observable deprecated in Java 9, and what does that history suggest about pub/sub API design generally?
drills.a: Observable is a concrete class (forcing single inheritance so you can't extend anything else), not thread-safe, and uses raw Object arguments from a pre-generics era. The general lesson: baking pub/sub into a base class you must extend (rather than composing it as a standalone EventBus/publisher object) is a design mistake independent of language -- it constrains your class hierarchy for a cross-cutting concern that should be composable.

drills.q: Design a state machine for an order lifecycle and explain precisely what the State pattern buys you over scattered if-statements.
drills.a: Model states as an enum (PENDING, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED) with an explicit transition table (dict/map of current state to allowed next states) checked on every transition attempt. This buys a single, auditable source of truth for legality -- a jump like PENDING to DELIVERED is a loud, caught error -- versus scattered if-checks where a missing branch silently allows an illegal transition. Full per-state subclasses with polymorphic handle() are only needed when each state has meaningfully different processing behavior, not just different allowed transitions.

drills.q: Map the saga pattern's orchestration-vs-choreography distinction onto GoF behavioral pattern names, and explain the risk of the orchestration side.
drills.a: Orchestration maps to Mediator: a central coordinator sequences and routes calls between services that never reference each other directly. Choreography maps to Observer/pub-sub: each service reacts to events with no central coordinator. The risk on the Mediator/orchestration side: the central coordinator can absorb all business logic over time and become a God Object, so it must be kept to pure routing/sequencing rather than embedding domain rules.

drills.q: Why doesn't naive Memento (deep-copying full object state per command) scale, and what do production undo systems and durable execution frameworks (Temporal, LangGraph) do instead?
drills.a: Deep-copying an entire large document/graph on every single command is a real memory and latency cost when state is large and commands are frequent (e.g. per keystroke). Production systems instead store the inverse command (undo by reversing the last Command) or incremental diffs, falling back to full snapshots only at coarser checkpoints -- exactly what LangGraph/Temporal checkpointers do when persisting enough state to resume a run after a crash without serializing everything on every step.
